summary: Offers advice to people designing link layers and local networks that must carry Internet protocols. It explains how design choices such as packet size, error handling and delay affect how well IP and TCP work, drawing on lessons from past designs. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC advises designers of link layers and local networks on choices that affect IP and TCP. It explains how packet size, errors, delay and other link features can change Internet performance.

questions: how link design affects tcp performance
what mtu should a new link use
subtitle: Design guidance for link layers and local networks that carry IP and TCP traffic.

tldr.problem: Link-layer design choices about packet size, loss, delay, buffering and routing can affect Internet protocols even when the link successfully carries IP packets.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reviews the features and trade-offs subnetworks should consider when supporting IP, including MTU, framing, broadcast, multicast, retransmission, congestion, compression and security.
tldr.outcome: It is Best Current Practice BCP 89. The memo emphasizes keeping subnetwork features limited where possible and leaving end-to-end reliability and security to endpoints; RFC 9599 later updated it.

facts.label: Recommended error detection
facts.value: At least as strong as a 32-bit CRC

today: RFC 3819 is a Best Current Practice published in July 2004. It has been updated by RFC 9599, so read the two RFCs together.

sections.title: Who the Guidance Is For
sections.content:
The RFC is for designers of communication equipment, link-layer protocols and packet-switched local networks that carry Internet protocols. It calls these networks subnetworks: Layer 2 networks immediately below IP that do not use IP routers to forward packets internally.

Designing a subnetwork for IP means providing enough features to carry IP, avoiding unnecessary complexity, and choosing parameters that support Internet performance. The document repeatedly applies the end-to-end principle: endpoints remain responsible for reliable delivery and end-to-end security.

Some lower-layer functions can improve performance in particular conditions, such as retransmission on a lossy mobile radio link. Designers should understand how such functions interact with the higher layers.
sections.plainLanguage: This guidance is for people building the network layer immediately below IP. It asks them to support IP without duplicating functions that endpoints already perform, unless a clear benefit justifies the extra mechanism.

sections.title: MTU, Fragmentation and Framing
sections.content:
A subnetwork's Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) is its largest supported packet. The RFC says router fragmentation is best avoided: IPv4 hosts must accept 576-byte packets, and IPv6 requires a minimum MTU of 1280 bytes. A subnetwork whose internal payload is smaller than 1280 bytes needs its own fragmentation and reassembly if it is to carry IPv6.

Slow links create a trade-off between packet size and serialization delay. An MTU-sized 1500-byte packet takes about 8 milliseconds on a T1 link at 1.536 Mb/s, but 625 milliseconds at 19.2 kb/s. A 256-byte MTU reduces that transmission time to a little over 100 milliseconds, though small packets increase header overhead.

IP also needs the subnetwork to mark variable-length packet boundaries. Fixed-size units need an adaptation method, such as padding and marking the last unit, carrying a pointer to the end of the packet, or inserting a flag between packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Large packets use link capacity efficiently but can take too long to send on a slow link. The designer must balance transmission delay, header overhead and the minimum packet sizes IP requires.

sections.title: Connections, Broadcast and Multicast
sections.content:
IP is connectionless, while some subnetworks create connections as traffic arrives and close them after an idle timeout. Because Internet traffic is bursty, a short timeout can cause frequent connection setup and a long timeout can waste resources. The RFC describes purely connectionless subnetworks as a natural fit for best-effort IP.

Shared links should support native broadcast because IPv4 protocols such as ARP, RARP, BOOTP, DHCP and RIP use it. A lack of broadcast can slow or prevent some functions, including DHCP. IPv6 uses multicast for related tasks.

Native multicast lets a subnetwork send one copy to group members rather than sending a separate copy to each member or broadcasting to all nodes. Switched subnetworks need a way to deliver multicast to group members, such as flooding or using group-membership information.
sections.plainLanguage: Some IP protocols need broadcast to discover devices or configure addresses. Native multicast lets a network deliver a packet to group members without sending a separate copy to every member.

sections.title: Reliability and Error Detection
sections.content:
Endpoints have ultimate responsibility for recovering from lost, corrupted, duplicated or reordered packets. The RFC therefore recommends lightweight subnetwork reliability rather than trying to make each link perfectly reliable. Automatic Repeat Request (ARQ) detects errors and requests retransmission; Forward Error Correction (FEC) adds redundancy so some errors can be corrected without retransmission.

Link-layer retransmissions can increase delay enough to trigger an unnecessary TCP retransmission. When a link cannot distinguish flows, its ARQ persistency should be small. When it can distinguish flows, the RFC recommends high persistency for reliable transports such as TCP and low persistency for other flows; it notes a practical upper limit of 30 to 60 seconds.

A subnetwork designed for IP should detect errors at least as strongly as a 32-bit CRC. End-to-end checksums remain necessary because host or router faults can corrupt data too. For applications that tolerate corrupted payloads, the RFC notes UDP-Lite as a transport that can support partial payload protection.
sections.plainLanguage: Link retransmission can improve delivery but may interfere with TCP's own recovery. The link should detect corruption strongly, while endpoints retain responsibility for end-to-end reliability.

sections.title: Effects on TCP and Queues
sections.content:
TCP treats packet loss as a possible sign of congestion. It reduces its sending rate after loss and increases the rate when acknowledgments arrive. Therefore, packet loss, delay and delay variation on a subnetwork can reduce TCP throughput or slow recovery.

When traffic exceeds a link's capacity, queues absorb bursts but add delay. The RFC discusses Active Queue Management as a way to signal congestion before queues are full and describes RED as one example; it notes that algorithm performance depends on configuration and conditions. Buffer capacity and queue-management policy should be considered together.

The RFC also explains that asymmetric bandwidth can slow the return of TCP acknowledgments, and packet reordering can cause TCP to mistake reordered packets for loss. Designers should avoid reordering when practical, but not at the cost of efficiency, reliability or delay.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP interprets packet loss as congestion, and long or variable delays affect its recovery. Queue management, adequate buffering and careful handling of acknowledgments and packet order can improve performance.

sections.title: QoS, Compression, Mobility and Routing
sections.content:
The RFC describes Integrated Services for per-flow reservations and Differentiated Services for handling aggregates of traffic. A subnetwork may support bandwidth reservation, allow unused reserved capacity to be shared, and tell IP about fixed delay and jitter.

Subnetwork compression is usually not useful for application data that is already compressed or encrypted. The RFC strongly recommends header compression on low-speed links or links with small MTUs. Compression requires in-order delivery and packet loss can delay recovery of the shared context.

A subnetwork may support internal mobility, but wide-area routing should account for the physical layout and differing link characteristics. IP routing assumes multipoint subnetworks are stable and have uniform metrics among their members. Designers should reuse existing routing protocols when they can.
sections.plainLanguage: Subnetwork features can support quality of service, header compression and mobility, but each adds constraints. Routing must reflect the network's actual delay and topology rather than hide important differences from IP.

sections.title: Security Placement
sections.content:
The RFC's security placement principle says a security mechanism is most effective close to, and under the control of, the owner of the asset it protects. Subnetwork security cannot provide end-to-end confidentiality, authentication or integrity by itself. A weak lower-layer mechanism may give users a false sense of protection.

The RFC supports protecting subnetworks against theft of service and denial of service. It also recommends considering authentication of the source of a subnetwork frame, which can address weaknesses in address resolution. Designers should be especially careful when designing mechanisms intended to prevent traffic analysis.

The memo lists design and implementation mistakes including weak algorithms, security by obscurity, shared keys, clear-text passwords, insufficient key length, missing replay protection and failure to address man-in-the-middle attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Link security can protect the link, but it cannot replace security between the communicating endpoints. Designers should state the limits of lower-layer protection and guard the subnetwork itself.
